title: A launcher's leftovers tap also records the game, so game audio is in the clip twice
claim: In `Leftovers::assign` (audio/mod.rs:201-207) the coverage check `let covered = spoken_for.contains(&root) || ancestors(root, tree).iter().any(|parent| spoken_for.contains(parent));` only asks whether a leftovers root sits *below* something already recorded, never whether it sits *above* it. In addition, `SourceKind::Game => taken.extend(game_pid),` (mod.rs:289) excludes only the game pid itself, not `app_root(game_pid)`. Launchers (Steam, Battle.net, Epic, Riot Client) start the game as their child, and the repo's own test fixture notes steam.exe "holds sessions on every device". So steam.exe becomes a leftovers root and is tapped with `INCLUDE_TARGET_PROCESS_TREE`, which includes its child, the game. Same class: if the game's parent runs the same exe (a launcher stub), the leftovers tap that parent and record the game again.
scenario: User records a Steam game with a Game source plus an output device in leftovers mode. steam.exe is chosen as a leftovers root and its INCLUDE_TREE tap captures game.exe, so the game is on the game track and also in the device/main mix. Muting the game track afterwards no longer removes the game audio, which is exactly what the README promises cannot happen.
fix: In `assign`, also skip any root that is an ancestor of a taken pid: `taken.iter().any(|t| ancestors(*t, tree).contains(&root))`. For such a root, tap its other session-holding descendants one by one instead (accept that the launcher's own sound is lost, or surface a warning). Use `app_root` for the game in both `taken` and the tap. Add a test with steam.exe as the parent of game.exe.

I copied mod.rs unchanged into a scratch crate and ran resolve(): with tree {33264 steam.exe <- 12800 explorer, 5000 game.exe <- 33264} and spk sessions [(33264,false),(5000,true),(900,true)], game_pid=5000, the result was game=[5000], system=[900, 33264]. It also happens with no launcher at all when the foreground game pid has a parent running the same exe: app_root climbs to that parent and taps it. The code relies on that in devices.rs:109 and in its nesting test, but it cannot be checked from source here. title: Clips with one audio track: gain compounds on every save, and mute permanently strips the audio
claim: When a clip has no individual tracks (only one WAV at save time, e.g. "desktop audio only", or a legacy clip), `from_stems == false` and the audio comes from `format!("0:a:{}", track.index)` of input 0. When nothing is cut at the front, input 0 is the current clip file (`VideoSource::Clip`), which already has the previous gain baked in. The editor (ClipEditor.tsx:113-121) still shows a gain/mute row for that single track and `apply_clip_edit` stores the mix, so every later save re-applies it on top and adds one more AAC generation. A front cut instead reads the original, so the level jumps back. Muting the track makes `mix_filter` return `None`, which yields `-an`; without an original the audio is gone for good, `clip_tracks` then returns 0 tracks, so `dirty` (ClipPlayer.tsx:535) can never become true and Save is disabled for that clip forever. With an original present, later saves fail because `0:a:0` no longer exists in the target.
scenario: A desktop-audio-only clip: set the track to -6 dB and save; open again and save another edit -> audio is now -12 dB, and so on with an extra AAC generation each time. Or mute the track and save -> audio stripped permanently (no original) and Save is disabled for that clip forever; with an original, later saves fail on missing `0:a:0`.
fix: For single-track clips, always take the audio from `edit::source_path(clip)`, seeked to `stems_start_ms`, so it stays one generation from the original and the gain is relative to it. Alternatively, write a stem (a copy of the original track) on the first edit. Or hide/disable gain and mute when `!separate`, and store neutral values after baking them in.

Output devices default to the main mix (AudioMixer.tsx:30-31 `wantsOwnTrack` = `kind.type !== "outputDevice"`), so a desktop-audio-only setup always yields such clips. Then edit.rs:594 `from_stems = stem_files.len() == list.len() && !stem_files.is_empty()` is false, edit.rs:644 takes audio from `0:a:{index}` of input 0, and input 0 is the current clip when the front is not cut: edit.rs:299 `(false, _) => (VideoSource::Clip, 0)`, edit.rs:413 `VideoSource::Clip => target.clone()`. With a front cut and an original, input 0 is the original (`(true, true) => (VideoSource::Original, absolute_start)`), so the level snaps back. UI: ClipEditor.tsx:113 `{tracks.map((track) => (<TrackRow .../>))}` renders gain/mute/solo for the one track regardless of `separateTracks`; useClipMix.ts:128 `separate = tracks.length > 1 && ...`, and :280 `video.current.volume = separate ? 0 : master` means the preview ignores the slider. ClipPlayer.tsx:533 sends `mix.toRequest()`; commands.rs apply_clip_edit passes it straight to edit::apply and `store` saves it as clip.edit.tracks, so initialMix shows -6 dB again on reopen and any later trim re-applies it. Without a trim, plan.original is None so swap_in runs edit.rs:570-571 `if !keep_original { remove(&clip.id); }`, and nothing else holds the audio. On reopen clip_tracks -> tracks_in_file on a file with no audio returns [] -> ClipPlayer.tsx:537 `mix.tracks.length > 0 &&` keeps dirty false, so Save (disabled={busy || !dirty ...}) is off for good and the clip cannot be trimmed again.
votes.corrected_claim: Core claim holds: gain compounds and the AAC generations pile up whenever the front is not cut, and a front cut with an original jumps back to the gain relative to the original. One correction on the case with an original: later saves fail only when the track is audible again and the front is not cut, because `[0:a:0]` points into the stripped clip. Saves that keep it muted (-an), and saves that cut the front (read from the original), still go through. There is a second permanent-loss path the report missed. 'Undo trim' (restore_clip_original) re-applies the stored mute to the original (restore_plan.original = None, so `-an`), then swap_in calls remove(&clip.id) and deletes the original. The audio is gone, and Save is locked out from then on.
votes.reachable_by: The user's own ordinary use of the clip editor, with no other actor involved. Most likely in the default setup where only an output device (desktop audio) is captured: output devices go to the main mix by default, which gives single-track clips. It also hits legacy or imported single-track clips. Compounding needs one gain change and then any later saved edit, such as a trim at the end. Permanent audio loss needs mute plus Save (or mute, then Undo trim). The UI still shows the slider and mute for the single track and gives no warning.
votes.fix_assessment: Taking single-track audio from edit::source_path(clip), seeked to stems_start_ms, keeps the gain relative to one fixed source. But with no original that source is the clip itself, so it only helps if an untouched copy is kept: either write a stem or copy on the first edit, or archive the original on any audio change, not just on a trim. The simplest safe fix is to hide or disable gain and mute when !separate (and send a neutral mix). That also matches the preview, which already ignores the slider for single-track clips.

votes.reachable_by: Any local user editing a clip that has one audio track (desktop audio only, mic only, mic summed into the main mix, or a legacy clip) who moves the gain slider or presses mute and then saves. The gain compounds on any later save, including a trim of the end only. votes.fix_assessment: Option 1 (always read audio from source_path) is not enough on its own. Mix-only saves on an untrimmed clip never archive an original, so source_path is the overwritten file itself. When the original has been discarded, stems_start_ms is also the wrong offset into the clip file. Option 2 (write the single track as a stem, e.g. `-c:a copy` to stems/<id>/0.m4a plus write_index, from source_path before the first swap) is the correct fix and keeps the feature, at about 1.4 MB/min of storage. Clips that were already edited must have their stored mix reset to neutral when the stem is made from an already-baked file. Option 3 is the safest small fix: in edit::arguments, when !from_stems ignore the mix and map `0:a?` with `-c:a copy` (no gain, no -an, no extra AAC generation, no missing-stream failure); hide or disable TrackRow when !separateTracks; and store neutral tracks for such clips. Separately, remove the `mix.tracks.length > 0` condition from dirty so that a clip without audio can still be trimmed.

title: Endpoint loopback on 5.1/7.1 devices drops the centre and surround channels (game dialogue)
claim: The packet conversion in capture.rs:280-287 keeps only the first two channels: `if src_channels == 1 { left = sample; right = sample; } else if channel == 0 { left = sample; } else if channel == 1 { right = sample; }`. There is no downmix of centre/LFE/surround channels. Device mode (endpoint loopback) is what "Quick setup" creates (default output device + mic; AudioMixer.tsx:506-511).
scenario: A gaming headset exposes a 7.1 endpoint (virtual surround). The game puts dialogue on the centre channel, which never reaches the clip; rear and side effects are lost too.
fix: Either initialise the device client with `float_format()` and `AUDCLNT_STREAMFLAGS_AUTOCONVERTPCM | AUDCLNT_STREAMFLAGS_SRC_DEFAULT_QUALITY` so Windows does the downmix and resampling, or implement an ITU downmix driven by `dwChannelMask`.

votes.evidence: capture.rs:335-354 device_client: `let mix = client.GetMixFormat()?; let format = read_format(mix); ... client.Initialize(AUDCLNT_SHAREMODE_SHARED, AUDCLNT_STREAMFLAGS_LOOPBACK, ..., mix, None)` -- the stream is opened in the endpoint's native mix format (6/8 ch on a 5.1/7.1 endpoint), no AUTOCONVERTPCM, no forced stereo. read_format (capture.rs:223-234) carries `channels: wf.nChannels`. convert (capture.rs:280-287): `if src_channels == 1 { left = sample; right = sample; } else if channel == 0 { left = sample; } else if channel == 1 { right = sample; }` -- channels 2..N (FC, LFE, BL, BR, SL, SR) are read and discarded. No dwChannelMask/downmix code anywhere in src-tauri (grep). Entry point: AudioMixer.tsx:500-511 QuickSetup adds `{ type: "outputDevice", deviceId: output.id }` for the default output (also shown in onboarding, Setup.tsx:284); its doc says "Game audio is left out on purpose: the output already carries it." audio/mod.rs:330 `SourceKind::OutputDevice { .. } if leftovers_mode => out.extend(leftovers())` -- only when a Game/Process-include source exists does the device become stereo process taps (process_client uses float_format(), 2 ch); otherwise capture.rs:513 `SourceKind::OutputDevice { device_id, .. } => device_client(device_id, true)` runs endpoint loopback.
votes.reachable_by: Ordinary use by the user: default Quick setup / onboarding (desktop audio + mic, no Game source) on any endpoint whose Windows speaker configuration is 5.1/7.1 -- many USB gaming headsets with 7.1 virtual surround, HDMI AV receivers/TVs, surround speaker sets. A game rendering to that mix format puts dialogue on FC and effects on rear/side channels, all dropped from every clip; stereo apps (Discord, browser) are unaffected. Not hit once a Game or Process-include source is added (leftovers mode converts the device to stereo process taps), nor on stereo-configured endpoints.
votes.fix_assessment: An ITU-style downmix keyed on dwChannelMask (FC*0.707 to both, surrounds*0.707 to their side, LFE dropped or attenuated) in convert() is the robust fix and also replaces the crude linear resampler; requesting a 2ch/48k float format with AUTOCONVERTPCM|SRC_DEFAULT_QUALITY on the loopback client is simpler but should be tested on real 7.1 endpoints since loopback+autoconvert behaviour varies, and it must still fall back to the mix format if Initialize rejects it.

votes.evidence: src-tauri/src/audio/capture.rs:330-336 device_client: `let mix = client.GetMixFormat()?; let format = read_format(mix); ... client.Initialize(AUDCLNT_SHAREMODE_SHARED, flags /* LOOPBACK only */, 200*REFTIMES_PER_MS, 0, mix, None)`, so the stream runs in the endpoint's own mix format (8 ch float on a 7.1 endpoint). read_format (236-247) keeps nChannels and never reads dwChannelMask. convert (280-287): `if src_channels == 1 { left = sample; right = sample; } else if channel == 0 { left = sample; } else if channel == 1 { right = sample; }`, so channels 2..N (C, LFE, BL, BR, SL, SR) are read and thrown away. frame_bytes (559) = channels*bits/8, so the buffer stride is right and nothing else breaks; the extra channels are simply discarded. A grep for downmix/dwChannelMask/AUTOCONVERTPCM across src-tauri/src finds nothing. Reach: AudioMixer.tsx:506-509 QuickSetup adds `{ type: "outputDevice", deviceId: output.id }` for the default output, and the comment at 476-477 says "Game audio is left out on purpose: the output already carries it." So endpoint loopback is the default game-audio path. Process loopback (process_client, 403-411) asks for float_format() stereo, so a "Game" source avoids this.

title: Export-to-size truncates the duration to whole seconds and overshoots the target
claim: `export::recipe` computes `let seconds = (target.duration_ms / 1000).max(1);` (export.rs:79), which truncates the duration, so the bitrate budget is computed for a shorter clip than the real one.
scenario: A 15.8 s clip with a 10 MiB target is budgeted for 15 s and comes out at about 10.71 MB (+2.2%) before any encoder error; a 1.9 s clip is budgeted for 1 s and comes out nearly 2x over.
fix: Compute in ms: `video_bits * 1000 / duration_ms / 1000`.

Caller commands.rs:1102-1108 passes the real probed `duration_ms` and nothing else clamps or rounds it; video_kbps is only floored (`budget.max(200)`, export.rs:97), never capped. Trims can be as short as 200 ms (edit.rs:46 `MIN_LENGTH_MS: u64 = 200`). Recomputed with the code's own integer arithmetic: 10 MiB / 15.8 s -> budgeted for 15 s, 5296 kbit/s video + 128 audio = 10,712,400 bytes of stream (+2.16% over 10,485,760, before real container overhead, the 3% reserve already being spent); 10 MiB / 1.9 s -> budgeted for 1 s, 81,241 kbit/s -> 19.3 MB (1.84x). ExportDialog.tsx:36 preview uses `Math.round(clip.durationMs / 1000)` instead, so the UI and core also disagree.
votes.reachable_by: Any user exporting a clip (Export dialog presets 10/25/100 MB) or a share link that has to shrink (links.rs TARGET_BYTES 46 MiB) whose length is not a whole number of seconds; worst for clips of 1-3 s, where a short trimmed clip that already fit can be inflated to nearly twice the target.
votes.fix_assessment: Right direction but incomplete as written: both the audio cost (128 * duration_ms bits) and the division must use milliseconds (video_bits * 1000 / duration_ms / 1000, guarding duration_ms == 0), and ExportDialog.tsx preview() must be changed in step; capping video_kbps at the source bitrate would also stop short clips from being inflated.

title: First cut across drives: a crash during the copy makes `repair` mark the untouched clip as trimmed
claim: `move_across` (edit.rs:497-511) uses `std::fs::copy(from, to)` straight onto `video.mp4` in the originals store. When clips are on D: and AppData on C: (the case the README describes), copying several GB takes seconds to minutes. If the app is killed during the copy, on restart target, note and a partial `video.mp4` all exist and the DB row has no `original`, which matches repair arm `(true, Some(note), true) if clip.original.is_none()` ("swapped, but the database never got its turn", edit.rs:945-948), so `set_original(note)` runs; `settle` returns early because the clip's size is unchanged. Related: if the copy fails partway, swap_in (edit.rs:550-556) removes temp and note but leaves the partial `video.mp4`, and `source_path` (edit.rs:87-94) checks only that `video.mp4` exists, so it hands the partial file to later `clip_tracks` and edits until the next restart.
scenario: User makes a first front cut on a clip stored on D:, app is killed during the multi-GB copy to C:. On restart the DB says "trimmed at start_ms" while the file is the full recording, so the individual tracks play `start_ms` off the picture, and "Undo trim" works from a truncated archive with no moov (muxer does not use faststart) and fails.

In arm 3, check that the clip really is trimmed (probed length < `note.duration_ms` - tolerance) before trusting the note. Better: keep the originals store on the same volume as the clip (e.g. a hidden `.clippiboy/originals` folder) so the move is always an atomic rename, which also removes copying GBs to C: without checking free space.

After a kill mid-copy, repair edit.rs:921 `match (target.is_file(), note, video.is_file())` sees (true, Some, true), and edit.rs:945-948 `(true, Some(note), true) if clip.original.is_none() => set_original(&clip.id, Some(&note))` runs. Then settle edit.rs:846-848 `if actual_bytes == clip.size_bytes { return; }` returns early because the clip file was never touched, so the `is_the_whole_recording` check (edit.rs:853-856), which would have fixed it, never runs. The state lasts across restarts. Consequences: useClipMix.ts:139 `offset = clip.original.startMs` shifts the separate tracks against the full picture. Undo (edit.rs:369, restore_plan with VideoSource::Original) reads the truncated archive. The muxer writes originals without faststart (muxer.rs:304), so ffmpeg fails with no moov. Worse, a later back-only cut gives `archives_the_clip(true, ..)` = false (edit.rs:519), so replace_file overwrites the only full recording and only the truncated archive is left. Triggers: tray Quit calls `app.exit(0)` with no wait on WORKING (tray.rs:139-148); also power loss, a reboot, or any panic=abort (Cargo.toml:107).

The DB then says trimmed while the file is still the full recording. A second, smaller window gives the same outcome: after the copy finishes but before `remove_file(from)`, the archive is complete, so undo still works. The severity is overstated. It needs the clip folder on a different volume than %APPDATA% (the default Videos\ClippiBoy is usually on C:), the clip's first trim, and the process dying during the copy. For typical replay clips the copy takes about 1-6 s (hundreds of MB); only long manual recordings take longer. title: The activation completion handler can signal a closed event handle after a timeout
claim: On a 5 s activation timeout (capture.rs:177-192) `CloseHandle(event)` runs while the async operation still holds the completion handler (capture.rs:389-393), which holds the raw HANDLE; a late `ActivateCompleted` then calls `SetEvent` on a closed handle, which may since have been reused for another event (unsafe). Also, `Error::from_win32()` after `WAIT_TIMEOUT` reports GetLastError = 0 ("The operation completed successfully").
scenario: Process-loopback activation completes after the 5 s timeout: `SetEvent` hits a closed or reused handle, signalling an unrelated event; the timeout error is logged as "The operation completed successfully".
fix: Let the handler own the event (close it in `Drop`) and return an explicit timeout HRESULT.

votes.evidence: src-tauri/src/audio/capture.rs:177-180 `struct ActivationHandler { event: HANDLE }`; :186-188 `ActivateCompleted ... SetEvent(self.event)`; :355-357 handler built around a raw event; :382-387 `ActivateAudioInterfaceAsync(..., &handler)` (the system keeps its own reference to the handler until completion); :389-392 `if WaitForSingleObject(event, 5_000) != WAIT_OBJECT_0 { let _ = CloseHandle(event); return Err(windows::core::Error::from_win32()); }`. No cancel exists on IActivateAudioInterfaceAsyncOperation, so a late completion calls SetEvent on the closed handle value. Handle slots are recycled; other capture threads create events continuously (capture.rs:536 `CreateEventW` for the pump event). `Error::from_win32()` reads the thread's stale GetLastError; WaitForSingleObject does not set it on WAIT_TIMEOUT, so the reported text is whatever the previous call left, typically 0 -> 'The operation completed successfully'. (windows-core 0.58 source is not in ~/.cargo/registry here; this rests on its documented from_win32 = HRESULT::from_win32(GetLastError()).)
votes.reachable_by: A process-loopback source whose ActivateAudioInterfaceAsync completion takes longer than 5 s (audiosrv busy or hung). Rare; on a slow first activation, start() itself also gives up after its own 5 s recv_timeout (capture.rs:127).
votes.fix_assessment: Sound: give the handler ownership of the event (an Arc'd OwnedHandle closed in Drop, so it outlives the late callback), or leak and not close the handle on timeout. Return an explicit `HRESULT_FROM_WIN32(ERROR_TIMEOUT)`/`WAIT_TIMEOUT` error instead of `from_win32()`. Memory safety is not at stake (the handler object is refcounted); the hazard is signalling a recycled handle.

title: Leftovers mode spawns a thread and loopback client for every idle application holding a session

title: `AppState::new` applies audio config synchronously on the main thread at startup

title: AudioContext leaks if `createMediaElementSource` throws
claim: In `useClipMix.ts`, an AudioContext created inside the `try` block is not closed if `createMediaElementSource` throws.
scenario: Repeated failures leak AudioContexts (browsers limit how many can exist).
fix: No explicit fix given; implied: close the context in the error path.

also.title: AudioContext leaked if createMediaElementSource throws
also.claim: In useClipMix.ts:207-228, if `createMediaElementSource` throws after `new AudioContext()` succeeded, the AudioContext is never closed.
also.fix: Close the AudioContext in the error path.

Reachability is thin, though. The elements are always fresh for each effect run, because cleanup calls drop() → map.clear() (useClipMix.ts:178-185, 263) and build() then makes new Audio() objects. So the InvalidStateError that createMediaElementSource throws for an element already bound to a source cannot occur. If `new AudioContext()` itself throws (the 'no WebAudio' case the catch comment targets), nothing leaks. The effect does not retry in a loop: graphMode stays 'try' and it only reruns on tracks/separate/graphMode/video changes, so at most one context leaks per clip opening.

votes.fix_assessment: Hoisting `ctx` out of the try and calling `void ctx?.close().catch(() => undefined)` in the catch is correct and cheap.

title: `export_for_discord` reuses stale or half-written files and never fixes an oversize one
claim: `export_for_discord` (commands.rs:871-888) decides reuse with `let ready = std::fs::metadata(&output).map(|meta| meta.len() > 0 && meta.len() <= target_bytes)`: there is no freshness check against the source clip. `shrink` writes straight to the final file name, so a crash/kill leaves a truncated MP4 without moov that counts as "ready" from then on. Two quick presses run two ffmpeg processes with `-y` on the same file. An over-limit result is put on the clipboard regardless, and the next press re-encodes the same recipe and gets the same overshoot.
scenario: User exports for Discord, then trims or remixes the clip and exports again: the old export is copied to the clipboard. Or the app is killed mid-export: the truncated file is reused forever. title: Applications running elevated are stored as "PID n" and can never be found again
claim: The process name lookup in devices.rs:91-96 uses `OpenProcess(PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION | PROCESS_VM_READ)` plus `GetModuleBaseNameW`, which fails for elevated processes. The UI then stores `exe: "PID 1234"`.
scenario: User adds an elevated application as a source; after a restart `live_pid` cannot find "PID 1234" and the source silently drops out.
fix: Take the name from the `process_tree()` snapshot, or use `QueryFullProcessImageNameW`, which needs only limited query rights.

also.title: Audio process picker opens every audio-session process (including the game) with PROCESS_VM_READ
also.claim: The audio process picker (audio/devices.rs:91-98) opens every audio-session process, including the game, with `PROCESS_VM_READ`, which is an anti-cheat concern (game.rs, by contrast, uses only `PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION`).

When the non-elevated app cannot open a process with PROCESS_VM_READ (elevated, protected or anti-cheat-guarded), the picker stores exe "PID n". live_pid accepts the stored pid only when the snapshot exe name equals the stored exe, and the snapshot has the real name (e.g. game.exe). title: Meter peak uses load-then-store instead of `fetch_max`
claim: The meter peak update in ring.rs:130-133 uses an atomic load followed by a store instead of `fetch_max`, so concurrent updates can lose a higher peak.
scenario: A peak written between the load and the store is overwritten by a lower value, under-reporting the meter.
fix: Use `fetch_max`.

votes.evidence: ring.rs:130-133 `let previous = f32::from_bits(self.peak.load(Ordering::Relaxed)); if peak > previous { self.peak.store(peak.to_bits(), Ordering::Relaxed); }`. The only other access is take_peak ring.rs:231 `self.peak.swap(0, Ordering::Relaxed)`. Each ring has exactly one writer: engine.rs:110-111 `let ring = Arc::new(SampleRing::new(..)); match capture::start(&stream.kind, ring.clone())`, the ring is moved into one capture thread (capture.rs:113-121), and the only write call is capture.rs:656 `ring.write(&converted, qpc_100ns)`. take_peak is called only from levels() (engine.rs:234), which the 50 ms UI loop calls (lib.rs:965).
votes.corrected_claim: The claimed mechanism, a higher peak from another writer overwritten by a lower one, cannot happen: every ring has a single writer thread, so nothing else can store a peak between the load and the store. The race that does exist is with take_peak's swap(0). If the reset lands between the load and the compare, and the new block's peak is not above the value that was just read out, the store is skipped. That one block's (~10 ms) peak is then missing from the next meter reading. The effect is a briefly under-reported level meter and nothing more; recorded audio is unaffected.
votes.reachable_by: A capture thread and the UI level-meter loop interleaving, only while a window that shows meters is visible (or CLIPPIBOY_LOG_LEVELS is set).
votes.fix_assessment: Valid and simpler: `self.peak.fetch_max(peak.to_bits(), Ordering::Relaxed)` is correct because peak is a non-negative f32 (from abs(), NaN never passes the `>` check). For non-negative floats, ordering by u32 bit pattern matches ordering by value.

title: `plan` can produce a 200 ms excerpt starting at the very end of the file
claim: For very short trims, `edit::plan` can produce a 200 ms excerpt starting at the very end of the file, because the end is clamped past the duration.
scenario: User trims to a tiny range near the end; the render starts at/after EOF and yields an empty or broken excerpt.
fix: No explicit fix given in the report.

votes.evidence: src-tauri/src/edit.rs:280-288: `let start = trim.start_ms.min(clip_duration_ms); let end = trim.end_ms.clamp(start + MIN_LENGTH_MS, clip_duration_ms.max(start + MIN_LENGTH_MS)); ... let absolute_end = offset + if cuts_back { end } else { clip_duration_ms }; let length_ms = absolute_end.saturating_sub(absolute_start).max(MIN_LENGTH_MS);`. Running a scratch copy of this arithmetic: trim (30000,30000) with D=30000 gives abs=(30000,30000), len=200, video_start=30000, trimmed=true, i.e. a 200 ms render starting exactly at EOF plus a zero-length ClipOriginal. Trim (29950,30000) gives a 200 ms render from 29950, running 150 ms past the end. The IPC handler does no validation (commands.rs:1015 `let trim = edit::Trim { start_ms, end_ms };`). The shipped UI cannot produce such a trim, however: both handles keep a 0.5 s gap (PlayerControls.tsx:148-149 and ClipPlayer.tsx:453-454 `Math.min(at, current.end - 0.5)` / `Math.max(at, current.start + 0.5)`), the end is bounded by the element's duration, and restoreTrim clamps to the duration (ClipPlayer.tsx:1033-1037).
votes.corrected_claim: The cause is not really the end clamp. When `start` is within 200 ms of the end (or at it), cuts_back is false, so absolute_end falls back to clip_duration_ms. `.max(MIN_LENGTH_MS)` then forces a 200 ms length that runs past absolute_end, because `start` is clamped to clip_duration_ms rather than to clip_duration_ms - MIN_LENGTH_MS. The UI's 0.5 s minimum gap makes this unreachable unless the IPC is called directly, or the element's duration exceeds the DB duration_ms by more than about 0.3 s. For a clip that was already back-trimmed, the 200 ms would come from the original beyond the clip's end rather than from EOF.
votes.reachable_by: A direct apply_clip_edit invoke with start_ms >= duration_ms - 200, or a large mismatch between element.duration and clip.duration_ms. Not reachable through the trim handles.
votes.fix_assessment: Clamp start to `clip_duration_ms.saturating_sub(MIN_LENGTH_MS)` (and derive end from it), or reject trims shorter than MIN_LENGTH_MS in apply_clip_edit. Either is a one-line hardening.

title: Autoplay-blocked AudioContext leaves preview silent and the error is swallowed
claim: In `useClipMix.ts`, `ctx.state !== "running"` returns early, so an AudioContext blocked by autoplay stays silent while the video is muted, and `play().catch(() => undefined)` hides that failure.
scenario: The webview blocks the AudioContext from starting; the preview plays with no sound at all and nothing is reported.
fix: No explicit fix given in the report.

votes.evidence: The code facts hold: the watchdog bails out at useClipMix.ts:242 `if (!element || element.paused || built.ctx.state !== "running") return;`, so a context that never runs is never declared dead; resume and play errors are swallowed (useClipMix.ts:325 `ctx.resume().catch(() => undefined)`, :327 `audio.play().catch(() => undefined)`). The autoplay gate is also real in the main window: tauri.conf.json:27 sets its own `additionalBrowserArgs`, which replaces wry's default that would add `--autoplay-policy=no-user-gesture-required` (wry-0.55.1/src/webview2/mod.rs:294-302). The silent-preview scenario still needs the video to play while the AudioContext is refused, though. The <video> autoplays unmuted (ClipPlayer.tsx:730 `autoPlay`, no `muted`; video.volume is only set to 0 after the tracks arrive, useClipMix.ts:280). resume() is retried on every play/playing event (useClipMix.ts:322-337, 355). Under Chromium's document-user-activation policy, unmuted media and AudioContext pass through the same sticky-activation check, so a video that is allowed to play implies a context that can be resumed. Falling back would not help either: plain unmuted <audio>.play() is gated the same way.
votes.corrected_claim: The watchdog cannot detect a context stuck in 'suspended' and the failures are silent, but given the shared autoplay gate this does not produce a silently playing video. It only would if WebView2 allowed the unmuted <video> to play while refusing AudioContext.resume() after a play event.
votes.reachable_by: Only a WebView2 build whose autoplay decision for AudioContext differs from the one for unmuted media elements. That cannot be checked here because no Chromium/WebView2 source is present.
votes.fix_assessment: No fix was proposed. If wanted, log or surface a context that is still 'suspended' a few seconds after a play event; letting the watchdog fall back would not restore sound, because the plain-audio route is gated the same way.

title: Export target computed in MiB while Discord may enforce decimal MB
claim: The export target size is computed in MiB. If Discord enforces decimal MB, "10 MB" exports land 4.9% over the limit.
scenario: A "10 MB" Discord export is 10 MiB = 10.49 MB and is rejected by Discord's upload limit.
fix: No explicit fix given; implied: compute the target in decimal MB.

votes.evidence: The MiB arithmetic is not in export.rs. export.rs:39-41 takes a byte count (`pub bytes: u64`), and its MiB constant only appears in the tests (export.rs:206 `const MB: u64 = 1024 * 1024;`). Production targets are binary. commands.rs:872 has `let target_bytes = megabytes * 1024 * 1024;` (export_for_discord). src/components/ExportDialog.tsx:12 has `const MB = 1024 * 1024;`, used at :109 `api.exportClip(clip.id, targetMb * MB, output)` with presets 10/25 MB labelled Discord/Nitro (:18-22). Budget: export.rs:66 reserves 3% for container overhead, so the stream aims at roughly 10,171,000 bytes for a '10 MB' target. That would exceed a decimal 10,000,000-byte limit but stays under a 10,485,760-byte one. Whether Discord enforces 10^6 or 2^20 cannot be checked from source; discord.com was unreachable from this sandbox. As far as I know, Discord's limits have always been binary (8 MiB = 8,388,608 B; 25 MiB = 26,214,400 B), and its developer docs state the upload limits in MiB.
votes.corrected_claim: The binary target is set in commands.rs:872 and ExportDialog.tsx:12, not in export.rs. It is only a defect if Discord enforces decimal megabytes. If the limit is 10 MiB / 25 MiB, as Discord's own documentation and long-observed byte limits suggest, the current arithmetic matches exactly and nothing lands over.
votes.reachable_by: A user choosing the 10 MB or 25 MB Discord preset, or export_for_discord. It only matters if Discord's server-side check is decimal.
votes.fix_assessment: Switching to decimal MB would shrink every export by about 4.6% for no gain if Discord uses MiB, which is likely. Confirm Discord's byte limit before changing anything. If it is decimal, change commands.rs:872 and ExportDialog.tsx:12 together so the preview matches.

title: Export starvation check assumes 30 fps
claim: The starvation check uses `bitrate_for(.., 30)` (export.rs:89), assuming 30 fps regardless of the clip's real frame rate, so the check is 2x too optimistic for 60 fps clips.
scenario: A 60 fps clip is judged to have enough bitrate at a resolution where it is actually starved, producing a visibly poor export.
fix: Use the real fps; consider stepping to 30 fps before dropping resolution.

title: One-pass ABR/CBR export leaves only a 3% size margin
claim: Export-to-size uses one-pass ABR/CBR with only a 3% margin, and the result is not verified against the target size.
scenario: Encoder rate-control error exceeds 3%, so the exported file is over the target size (e.g. over Discord's limit).
fix: Use x264 two-pass, or verify the result and re-encode with `bitrate × target/written × 0.97` when it is over.

title: The resampler is stateless and per packet, with no anti-aliasing
claim: The linear resampler in capture.rs:298-312 restarts the phase at 0 on each packet, and `next` is clamped inside the packet, so the last samples are held instead of interpolated into the next packet. `target_frames = (frames as f64 * ratio) as usize` truncates, dropping up to one frame per packet, which the ring's slew then has to absorb. There is no anti-aliasing filter.
scenario: 96/192 kHz endpoints (common "studio quality" settings) are decimated by picking samples, which aliases; 16/8 kHz Bluetooth HFP mics produce imaging; packet boundaries introduce small discontinuities and dropped frames.
fix: Use the AUTOCONVERTPCM + SRC_DEFAULT_QUALITY flags (as for the multichannel downmix issue), or a stateful resampler (`rubato`) kept per stream.

title: A single bad timestamp inserts silence and then shifts the source late for tens of seconds
claim: In `SampleRing` (ring.rs:151-163) any block whose stamp is over 50 ms late is treated as a real gap and immediately filled with zeros; the correctly stamped blocks that follow show negative drift, which may only slew at 2000 ppm (50 ms takes about 25 s). Negative drift between -50 ms and -1 s is never treated as a discontinuity. In capture.rs:631-657, `AUDCLNT_BUFFERFLAGS_TIMESTAMP_ERROR` (0x4) is ignored (only SILENT 0x2 is handled), and for devices on the fallback clock the read-time `now` is used as the stamp.
scenario: After a capture thread stall on a fallback-clock device, the first packet of the burst looks "late" and the rest "early": spurious silence is inserted even though WASAPI kept the data, and the source then plays ~50 ms late for ~25 s. Same with a single packet flagged TIMESTAMP_ERROR.
fix: Detect real gaps with `pu64DevicePosition` (pass it instead of `None`), which jumps by exactly the missing frames; ignore stamps flagged 0x4; with the fallback clock use `now − (GetCurrentPadding + frames)/rate`; require two agreeing blocks before filling a gap and re-anchor on a sustained negative drift; add tests for these cases.

title: No MMCSS, and the 80 ms mixer lag discards late packets
claim: Capture threads (capture.rs:470-499) and the mixer thread run at normal priority with no `AvSetMmThreadCharacteristicsW` (MMCSS). The mixer reads with an 80 ms lag (`AUDIO_LAG`, pipeline.rs:42); a packet that lands in the ring after the mixer has already pushed zeros for that window is lost from the clip.
scenario: Under game load a capture thread is delayed more than about 70 ms; its packet arrives after the mixer has written silence for that window, so audio that WASAPI kept is missing from the clip.
fix: Register the threads with MMCSS ("Audio"/"Capture"); raise `AUDIO_LAG` to about 200-250 ms (a replay buffer does not need low latency; the save can wait for the mixer to pass the last frame's QPC).

title: `snapshot()` hands over live TrackRings with only 2 s slack; front of clip audio may scroll out before being read
claim: `snapshot()` hands over the *live* `TrackRing`s, which keep only 2 s of slack, and the WAVs are only written after the whole h264 file has been written. The audio windows are not copied inside `snapshot()`.
scenario: A slow disk plus aligning the clip start to a keyframe delays the WAV writing long enough that the front of the clip's audio scrolls out of the live ring before it is read.
fix: Copy the windows inside `snapshot()`.

title: Sources set to "the default device" do not follow default-device changes
claim: There is no `IMMNotificationClient` (grep-confirmed). An empty `device_id` (capture.rs:320-327) binds to whatever was the default at stream start and stays there until that device becomes invalid. The fingerprint `out:` never changes, so the stream is never restarted. The configuration warning even claims the source "follows the Windows default device".
scenario: User switches the Windows default output from speakers to a headset while recording; the default-device source keeps recording the speakers endpoint.
fix: Register `OnDefaultDeviceChanged` and restart the affected stream.

title: Leftovers catch-all rule never matches a source configured as the default device ("")
claim: In `Leftovers::assign` (mod.rs:235) the catch-all rule compares `*device == self.default_device`; for a source configured as "the default device" `device` is `""` while `default_device` is the real endpoint id, so the catch-all never matches such a source.
scenario: An output source set to the default device in leftovers mode: applications "playing nowhere in particular" are not assigned to it via the catch-all rule.
fix: Normalise `""` to the resolved default device id before assigning.

title: Drawing the waveform holds the whole decoded audio in RAM; no per-clip lock; muted clips re-run ffmpeg
claim: The waveform uses ffmpeg's `showwavespic` (preview.rs:49-53), which queues every input frame until EOF (s16 mono), about 345 MB per hour of recording. There is no lock, so StrictMode/double opens write the same PNG concurrently; a long waveform job also keeps the clip open. Fully muted clips (no audio stream) re-run ffmpeg and error on every open.
scenario: Opening a 1-hour clip uses ~345 MB for the waveform; a save during a long waveform job fails with "is it open somewhere"; a double open writes the PNG concurrently; a muted clip errors on every open.
fix: Put `aresample=8000`/`asetnsamples` before `showwavespic`, or compute min/max peaks in Rust from `-ac 1 -ar 4000 -f s16le pipe:1`; add a per-clip lock.

title: Preview sync tolerates up to 120 ms offset and corrects with audible hard seeks
claim: In `useClipMix.ts`, tracks are only corrected when off by more than 120 ms (line 317), with a hard seek once a second (line 353). An A/V offset of up to 120 ms persists, and each correction is an audible skip.
scenario: During preview, track audio drifts up to 120 ms from the video without correction, then jumps audibly when re-seeked.
fix: Use a threshold of about 30-40 ms and nudge `playbackRate` by ±1-3% for small corrections, seeking only above about 150 ms. Or decode the tracks into AudioBuffers and schedule them against `ctx.currentTime`.

also.title: Stem drift correction is coarse and uses hard seeks
also.claim: `align()` re-seeks the stems only when drift exceeds 0.12 s (useClipMix.ts:317), checked once per second (line 353). Up to 120 ms of lip-sync error stays, and each correction is a hard seek.
also.fix: Correct drift by nudging `playbackRate` (+/-1-2 %) and hard-seek only above about 250 ms.

title: Preview silence watchdog trips on genuine silence or buffering and permanently switches route
claim: The silence watchdog in useClipMix.ts:238-252 trips on two seconds of genuine digital silence (AAC of zeros decodes to exact zeros) or on elements still buffering, and then permanently switches to the attenuate-only route.
scenario: A clip starting with 2 s of silence (or slow buffering) makes the preview permanently fall back to the attenuate-only route, losing the WebAudio gain graph.
fix: Switch only if no sample was non-zero since the graph was built.

also.title: Stem-preview silence watchdog mistakes real silence for a broken audio graph
also.claim: useClipMix.ts:246-251 `quiet = samples.some((value) => value !== 0) ? 0 : quiet + 1; if (quiet >= SILENT_TICKS) { ... setGraphMode("off"); }` (8 ticks of 250 ms = 2 s) is meant to catch a CORS-silent `MediaElementSource`, but stems are often digitally zero (game loopback in menus or pauses, a noise-gated mic). Two seconds of real silence while playing switches the clip permanently to the `volume` fallback, losing the +dB preview (other tracks get quieter instead), and all audio elements are rebuilt mid-playback, which is audible as a glitch.
also.fix: Detect the CORS case deterministically, e.g. `fetch(url, { mode: "cors", method: "HEAD" })` once, or decide only during the first seconds and only if the video's own audio is not silent.

title: An application picked by a child pid (Discord) records only that child; the other session is recorded nowhere
claim: In `audio::resolve`, `taken` excludes `app_root(live_pid)` (the whole Discord process tree) from the leftovers (mod.rs:292-298), but the application stream taps `pid: now`, the live pid itself (mod.rs:336-345). `list_processes` returns *session* pids, and for Discord those are its utility children (the repo's own `discord()` fixture); the UI stores one of them (AudioMixer.tsx:787-795).
scenario: User adds "Discord" by clicking one of its entries in the picker (a utility child pid). The sibling Discord session (voice or notifications/stream, depending on which entry was clicked) ends up neither on the Discord track nor in the leftovers, so it is not recorded at all.
fix: Tap `app_root(live_pid)` in `resolve`, consistent with `taken`. Also deduplicate the process picker by root.

title: A capture-start timeout leaves a zombie capture thread and WASAPI client running forever
claim: On the start timeout (capture.rs:127-136) the code returns `Err(_) => Err("timed out starting the audio source".into()),` without setting `stop`, and the JoinHandle is dropped. If the device's `Activate`/`Initialize` answers after 5 s, the thread sends into a dead channel and then pumps into an unreferenced ring forever, holding the WASAPI client. `retry_failed` runs every 10 s and can pile these threads up.
scenario: A flaky/slow USB or Bluetooth device takes more than 5 s to initialise; each 10 s `retry_failed` attempt times out and leaves another capture thread and client running indefinitely.
fix: Call `stop.store(true, Relaxed)` before returning the timeout error; the thread checks it after init and exits.

title: Solo counts disabled sources and is persisted: a disabled soloed source silences every track
claim: The audibility rule in audio/mod.rs:448-451 is `let any_solo = sources.iter().any(|s| s.solo); source.enabled && !source.muted && (!any_solo || source.solo)`. `any_solo` also counts disabled sources, and solo is stored in the config, so the state survives restarts. Solo is destructive (affects what is recorded, not just monitoring).
scenario: User solos a source, then disables it: every remaining track records silence, and this persists across restarts because solo is saved in the config.
fix: Use `sources.iter().any(|s| s.enabled && s.solo)`. Clear solo on disable and/or on startup. Add a configuration warning "solo active — N tracks record silence".

title: Level meters ignore solo and keep moving while the buffer records zeros
claim: `levels()` (audio/engine.rs:242) checks only `muted`, not `audible()`, so a source silenced by another source's solo still shows live meter levels.
scenario: A solo is active on another (possibly disabled) source; the meters of the non-soloed sources keep moving while their tracks record silence, so the user does not notice.
fix: Make the meters follow `audible()`.

title: Preview elements recreated after the fallback route never get the current `playbackRate`
claim: In `useClipMix.ts`, `<audio>` elements recreated after falling back to the old route never receive the current `playbackRate` until the next `ratechange` event.
scenario: User plays the preview at a non-1x speed, the hook falls back and recreates elements; the tracks play at 1x while the video plays at the chosen speed, drifting apart.
fix: No explicit fix given; implied: apply the current `playbackRate` when creating the elements.

votes.evidence: src/lib/useClipMix.ts:190-198 build() creates `new Audio()` without copying playbackRate, and the only place a rate is applied is the ratechange handler (useClipMix.ts:332-334 `audio.playbackRate = element.playbackRate`, :350). But nothing in the app ever changes the video's rate: `grep playbackRate|ratechange` over src/ hits only useClipMix.ts. The <video> in ClipPlayer.tsx:725-736 has no `controls` attribute (so no native speed menu), fullscreen goes to the container (ClipPlayer.tsx:414 `frame.current?.requestFullscreen()`), the keyboard map (ClipPlayer.tsx:470-499) has no speed keys, and the native context menu is suppressed app-wide (lockdown.ts:102 `window.addEventListener("contextmenu", (event) => event.preventDefault())`, installed in main.tsx:8). The video therefore always plays at 1.0, which is also the default for freshly created Audio elements.
votes.corrected_claim: Latent only: newly created track elements (on first build as well as after the fallback, not only after the fallback) start at playbackRate 1 and only follow the video on a later ratechange. The app has no way to set a non-1x rate, so this cannot desync anything today.
votes.reachable_by: Nobody through the shipped UI; only by setting video.playbackRate from devtools (which are blocked in production builds by lockdown.ts:55-57).
votes.fix_assessment: Calling rate() once in the sync effect's setup (before the `if (!element.paused) play()` at useClipMix.ts:355), or setting audio.playbackRate in build(), would close the gap cheaply if a speed control is ever added; it is not needed now.

title: Colour metadata (VUI) is not carried over on re-encode
claim: When a first cut re-encodes, `-colorspace`/`-color_primaries`/`-color_trc` are not set, so the colour metadata (VUI) of the source is not carried over.
scenario: A trimmed clip may display with different colours than the original in players that rely on VUI.
fix: No explicit fix given; implied: pass the source's colour metadata via `-colorspace/-color_primaries/-color_trc`.

votes.evidence: edit.rs:661-662 maps the video straight through (`-map 0:v:0`), with no video filter; the only filter_complex is the audio mix (edit.rs:654-657). video_args (edit.rs:714-741) adds only `-pix_fmt yuv420p` plus rate-control flags, which is accurate, but no explicit colour flags are needed: ffmpeg's CLI copies each decoded frame's colour_range/primaries/trc/colorspace into the encoder context when it opens the encoder. The sources are tagged at record time (mft.rs:535-538: MF_MT_YUV_MATRIX=BT709, NOMINAL_RANGE=16_235, TRANSFER_FUNCTION=709, VIDEO_PRIMARIES=BT709). Empirical check with local ffmpeg 6.1.1: a BT.709/tv-tagged source re-encoded with the app's exact arguments (`-ss 1.000 -i src.mp4 -map 0:v:0 -an -c:v libx264 -preset veryfast -pix_fmt yuv420p -crf 20 -avoid_negative_ts make_zero -movflags +faststart -t 2.000`) gives color_range=tv, color_space=bt709, color_transfer=bt709, color_primaries=bt709. The output SPS VUI has colour_description_present_flag=1 and primaries/transfer/matrix all 1. The same holds through a forced yuv444p->yuv420p conversion. The app ships ffmpeg 9.0.1 (tools.rs:30), which has the same encoder-setup behaviour.
votes.corrected_claim: Colour metadata is carried over on re-encode without explicit flags: ffmpeg passes the decoded frames' colour properties to the encoder, so the BT.709 limited-range tags the recorder writes come out in the trimmed clip's VUI. The only checks left are that the NVENC, AMF and QSV wrappers write VUI from those fields. This could not be tested here, but those FFmpeg wrappers do read avctx->colorspace, color_primaries and color_trc.
votes.reachable_by: Not reachable as described: any first cut with plan.reencode=true keeps the source's colour tags.
votes.fix_assessment: Not needed. Hard-coding -colorspace/-color_primaries/-color_trc would at best restate what ffmpeg already propagates, and would mis-tag any source that is not BT.709.
